title: How do you find the middle element of a linked list (slow/fast pointer)?
shortTitle: Find middle element of a linked list: slow/fast pointer
keyPoints: Slow pointer moves 1 step, fast pointer moves 2 steps per iteration
When fast reaches the end (null or null.next), slow is at the middle
O(n) time and O(1) space -- no need to know the list size beforehand
For even-length lists, slow points to the second of the two middle nodes
The same technique is used for Floyd's cycle detection algorithm
Streams are not ideal here because linked traversal requires mutable pointer state

s1_definition.oneliner: Use two pointers: slow advances one node per step, fast advances two nodes. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Slow pointer** moves one node forward each iteration: `slow = slow.next`.
- **Fast pointer** moves two nodes forward each iteration: `fast = fast.next.next`.
- When `fast == null` or `fast.next == null`, slow is at the middle of the list.
- **O(n) time, O(1) space**: single pass, no extra data structures, no need to know the list length.
- For even-length lists, slow lands on the second of the two middle nodes.
- This is the tortoise-and-hare algorithm, also used for cycle detection (Floyd's algorithm).
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, a queue of customers waits in line. One clerk (slow) processes one customer at a time. Another clerk (fast) processes two at a time. When the fast clerk finishes the entire queue, the slow clerk is exactly at the middle customer. That middle customer gets priority VIP service.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Linked list: 100 → 200 → 300 → 400 → 500

  Step 0: slow=100  fast=100
  Step 1: slow=200  fast=300
  Step 2: slow=300  fast=500
  Step 3: fast.next=null → STOP

  Middle = slow = 300 ✓

  Even list: 100 → 200 → 300 → 400

  Step 0: slow=100  fast=100
  Step 1: slow=200  fast=300
  Step 2: slow=300  fast=null → STOP

  Middle = slow = 300 (2nd of 2 middles)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The slow/fast pointer (tortoise-and-hare) finds the middle of a linked list in one pass. Slow advances one node, fast advances two nodes per iteration. When fast reaches the end (`null` or `null.next`), slow is at the middle. For even-length lists, slow points to the second middle node.

This technique is O(n) time and O(1) space, with no need to know the list size beforehand. The same core trick powers Floyd's cycle detection algorithm and finding the kth node from the end.

At National Bank of India, a transaction history stored as a linked list can find the median-position entry for an auditor in a single traversal without buffering the whole list into another structure.

Remember one sentence: slow moves one step, fast moves two steps, and when fast finishes, slow is at the middle.
